claims.text: Lower atomic size mismatch produces higher effective atomic diffusion barriers in multimetallic nanoparticles.
Higher effective atomic diffusion barriers preserve a single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures.
Increasing atomic size mismatch allows diffusion barriers to be overcome more readily.
Increasing atomic size mismatch enhances atomic diffusion, segregation, and eventual phase separation.
The initial Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Mn nanoparticles are equiatomic, homogeneous, and single-phase solid solutions.
Partially substituting Mn with Cu can incrementally increase atomic size mismatch while retaining near-equal atomic ratios.
Cu is slightly larger than Mn for purposes of the proposed atomic-size-mismatch intervention.
Atomic size mismatch influences local atomic diffusion barriers.
Local atomic diffusion barriers determine the propensity for surface or interface segregation.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically favors a mixed, single-phase state.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility sufficiently to overcome stabilization of the mixed state.
Enhanced atomic size mismatch lowers local diffusion barriers and facilitates segregation and phase separation.
Under identical thermal conditions, lower-mismatch nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous solid-solution structure better than higher-mismatch nanoparticles.
Retention of the homogeneous solid solution will appear as consistent high-temperature XRD patterns and uniform elemental distributions in TEM mapping.
Higher-mismatch nanoparticles will develop secondary phases or detectable elemental demixing earlier than the baseline nanoparticles.
There is a sufficiently high temperature at which diffusion barriers in the baseline nanoparticles are also overcome.
Below that high-temperature limit, increased mismatch should produce a detectable comparative loss of stability.
At extremely high temperatures, both the baseline and modified nanoparticles may eventually phase-separate.
